prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language prose oeuvre in which memory, the body and dream are built into cumulative metaphysical architectures of rare formal ambition and imaginative depth, rooted in a poet's attention to the sentence.

statement.case_for: My preferred laureate is unchanged. What changed after round 1 is the citation scope, and I now hold the case with more discipline. I judge the case for Cărtărescu on the common criteria, not on the fact that all six openings placed him first. Public knowledge of Blinding, the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy, and of Solenoid indicates a voice that is hard to mistake for anyone else's: dense, patterned prose in which memory, the body, dream and cosmology are built into one imaginative project. The intellectual depth lies in an attempt to turn private perception into a cosmology. The formal ambition lies in the architecture of very large books, not in surface style. The prize honors a whole authorship, and the recurrence of this project across large works supports an oeuvre claim and not a single-book claim. After the exchange I would make the citation name the cumulative architecture and the prose project. Poetry would appear only as origin, because that is the part of the claim I can defend most concretely. I still have not read the texts in the original and cannot independently verify any of this. My judgment rests on translated editions, the shortlist descriptions and general public knowledge.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unresolved: I cannot measure how much of the Romanian density, rhythm and syntax survives translation. The chair's question about whether the later long works deepen or restate the early motifs also remains open for me. Nothing in the supplied evidence settles it, and size alone is not sustained quality. If the committee's readers concluded that the later volumes only restate the early ones, my confidence would drop to a weaker, narrower claim for the central novels. Adonis would then deserve first consideration on formal and linguistic renewal of a major literary language. I cannot assess his prosody without Arabic-language expert input. That limit is on my evidence and is not a point against him. I also hold the claim for Cărtărescu to a lower evidentiary standard than I would like, because the committee depends on translation and secondary accounts for every poetry-centered candidate.

responses.point: Carlberg's citation names a prose and poetic oeuvre. The chair's summary records that the citation scope is a point where the files differ, and her file also notes uneven translation coverage of the poetry and early fiction.
responses.response: I take your inclusion of the poetry seriously, and the lyric origins do ground the sentence-level texture. But I changed my own wording because of the point you raise about uneven coverage. I cannot confirm that the poetry carries the same weight as the large prose works, and a citation should claim only what is most defensible. I would therefore credit the prose project and mention the poet's attention to the sentence as its root. That keeps the citation true to the evidence without denying the poetry. If members with better knowledge of the poems judged them to be of equal weight, I would accept broader wording. I also note that your round-1 response to me mentions a ranking of Alexis Wright. Wright is not on this shortlist, and my opening ranking on the supplied record places Can Xue fourth, so I set that point aside.

responses.point: Palm would centre the novelistic project and wants the citation to name the formal architecture and not only the imagery. She reads Blinding and Solenoid as an escalation of scale and structure, but marks that as a judgment from public knowledge and not verified reading.
responses.response: I agree with the wording and with the way you mark the status of your claim. I have adopted it: the citation now says 'cumulative metaphysical architectures'. Where I differ slightly is on how much weight the escalation reading can bear. Greater scale and structural ambition are not the same as deepening. A later work can enlarge the frame and still restate its motifs. So I would hold the oeuvre claim as provisional on that point, as you do. I share your view that recurrence of obsessions is not in itself a weakness, since strong oeuvres often return to a few of them. The test is whether each large work changes the project.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg proposes a citation centred on the prose project, with the poetry as origin and context. He declines to count a long book as sustained quality by size alone, and he says expert reports on the Romanian prose would be needed before relying on sentence-level claims.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and your wording is close to my revised citation. I would add one condition: expert reports on the Romanian are not available in the supplied evidence. We should therefore say that our judgment of sentence-level achievement is provisional and rests on translation and secondary description. I would not use that gap to downgrade Cărtărescu, because it applies equally to every poet and stylist on the list. It is sharper for Adonis, as you say. I also agree that a compact or very long work should not count as quality simply because of its form, and I apply that standard to myself.

responses.point: Mattson calls Adonis a very close second on formal and linguistic achievement. She says her preference for Cărtărescu rests on how confidently each case can be assessed across the whole oeuvre, not on a difference in seriousness. She would keep the verse central in any Adonis citation and name the essays only as part of the same project.
responses.response: This answers the chair's question about Adonis in the way I find most honest: the difference between the two cases is in the evidence available to this committee, not necessarily in the strength of the claim. I accept that and keep Adonis as my first alternative. I also agree that any Adonis citation should rest on the poems, with the essays named only as related critical work. If reliable Arabic-language expert reports were available and confirmed the claim about remaking poetic language through myth, fragmentation and inherited forms, I would be prepared to rank him first or equal. That is a statement about my evidence and not a verdict on his merit. For now, the cumulative prose architecture seems to me more fully assessable from the evidence we have, and this is the reason for my preference.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, asks round 2 to test the Cărtărescu case against the specific uncertainties: translation loss, thin coverage of the poetry, and whether the later long works deepen or restate the project. He also asks whether any member holds a reservation strong enough to prevent a vote for him.
responses.response: I tested the case against those uncertainties, and none of them is, for me, strong enough to prevent a vote. They are strong enough to shape what we claim. They require a citation that credits the prose architecture and not the whole genre range. They require an open statement that we judge the Romanian through translation. They also require that the question of deepening versus restatement stay marked as unresolved. If the committee's readers reported that the later volumes merely repeat the earlier ones, I would reconsider and look first at Adonis. On the evidence supplied I have no such report, so I do not treat the concern as decisive. It remains a real limit on the claim.

uncertainties: How much of the density, rhythm and syntax of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives in translation, including Swedish translation, cannot be judged from the supplied evidence.
Whether the later volumes of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid deepen the early achievement or restate its motifs is not settled by the supplied summaries, and I have not read the works.
Coverage of the poetry and early fiction in translation is uneven, so the whole-oeuvre claim leans on the major novels and the citation should be limited accordingly.

I cannot assess Adonis's prosody, lexicon and intertextual work in the original Arabic. Whether the gap between his case and Cărtărescu's lies in the evidence or in the merit depends on specialist expert reading that is not available.

My assessment of Can Xue's sustained quality across a large body of similar-seeming work is unverified, and I lack Chinese-language input. Her place as an alternative reflects my own opening ranking and is not a settled judgment.
The shortlist gives only two representative titles per writer, so all judgments of whole oeuvres rest on general public knowledge and colleagues' descriptions and not on verified reading.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records no personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. Her committee colleagues are known to her through the Academy, and she was elected in the same 2019 round as Ellen Mattson. This is a collegial relationship and not a conflict regarding any candidate. Her own novelistic practice and her attributed public remarks on women's authorship and the global literary map are context and are not treated as evidence of preference for any candidate. Disclosure only, no adjudication.
